header.totals_note: Site totals come from the date pull and page rows from the page pull. Search Console counts them slightly differently, so page rows do not add up exactly to the site totals.

summary: Site clicks were 10180 in the last 28 days: -17.8% on the quarter-ago window (12387), -1.5% on the previous 28 days (10340) and +7.9% on the same weeks last year (9434). Most of the fall came between the quarter-ago and the previous window, and it has slowed since.

8 pages lost at least 51 clicks and 30% of their baseline, 1713 clicks in all. 1127 of them sit on pages a refresh, rewrite, merge or review can win back; 229 are seasonal demand (/blog/slow-season-ideas/, where Trends shows 'salon slow season ideas' -75%), and 357 went with a redirect or with brand searches moving to the home page.

The biggest fixable losses: /blog/reduce-no-shows/ slipped from position 4.0 to 8.0 and was last updated 19 months ago, and /blog/appointment-reminder-templates/ held position 3.4 while its CTR fell from 8.8% to 4.1%, under a new AI Overview.

Neither Google update you asked about lines up with a drop (May 2026 core update: possible gain; June 2026 spam update: no clear effect). Your own blog template change on 2026-08-11 does: site clicks -11.7% in the 14 days after it against -0.9% before, with /blog -22.1% while the home page held (+4.2%). It is a 'possible hit' rather than a likely one because average position moved +0.6, under the 1-place bar.

ga4.note: GA4 recorded 8869 organic sessions against 10180 Search Console clicks in the same 28 days (87.1%), above the 50% floor, so its organic key events break ties and show which decaying pages convert.

wordpress.note: Content age is months since the WordPress 'modified' date, up to the last day with data. A rank-loss post not updated in 12 months or more leads its tier.

bing_control.note: Bing had 651 clicks in the current window, enough to act as a control. Bing fell 12.7% on the quarter-ago window and Google 17.8%: both fell, so the cause sits with demand or the site itself (the seasonal post and the blog template change), not with Google alone.

unknowns: Page-level seasonality: page rows were pulled for three windows, so a page's own clicks a year ago are not compared. The site-level year-ago window and Google Trends cover it.
